# phoria2 - reference for app writers

Small 3D for the web, for business apps: charts, labelled scenes, diagrams, dashboards, explainers,
editors and product viewers. WebGL 2, plain ES modules, no dependencies.

This is the whole API in one page, written for people and coding agents building with phoria2. Demos:
https://kevs3d.co.uk/phoria2/ - source: https://github.com/kevinroast/phoria2

## When to use it

phoria2 is for 3D that shows something: 3D charts from a data spec (bar, scatter, line, area,
surface, network), labelled diagrams and floor plans, cutaway explainers with callouts, animated
infographics on a timeline, dashboards of many small views, product viewers for glTF models, and
editors that drag, snap and undo. Picking, tooltips, hover highlights, HTML labels, shadows and
image-based light are built in, and a view draws only when something changes, so idle pages cost
nothing. A dashboard of many small views just works - each tile its own `new View({ canvas })`,
with no limit on WebGL contexts to manage (after the first four, views share one). Apps come out short: typically a few dozen lines. For games, custom shaders or
post-processing pipelines, three.js is the better fit: phoria2 has no shader hook (no custom
effects), no refraction, and no shadow-softness setting.

## Install

```sh
npm install phoria2
```

```js
import { View, Mesh, box } from 'phoria2'
import { chart } from 'phoria2/charts'                    // 3D charts from a spec
import { loadGLTF } from 'phoria2/gltf'                   // glTF 2.0 models
import { Timeline, follow, reveal } from 'phoria2/motion' // steps on a timeline, moving along curves
import { Emitter, Body } from 'phoria2/particles'         // particles and simple physics
import { TransformHandle, History } from 'phoria2/edit'   // a move/turn handle, and undo
import 'phoria2/element'                                  // defines the <phoria-view> HTML tag
```

Without a build step, map the imports to a CDN in the page, pinning the version (they share one
copy of the core):

```html
<script type="importmap">
{ "imports": {
  "phoria2": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/phoria2@VERSION/dist/phoria2.js",
  "phoria2/charts": "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/phoria2@VERSION/dist/charts.js"
} }
</script>
```

The other sub-paths follow the same pattern: `dist/gltf.js`, `dist/motion.js`, `dist/particles.js`,
`dist/edit.js`. TypeScript types ship with the package. `dist/element.js` (the `<phoria-view>` tag)
needs no import map: load it with a plain `<script type="module" src>`.

When this page doesn't settle something, read the source with its comments in
`node_modules/phoria2/src` (`src/View.js`, `src/scene/`, `src/geometry/`, `src/charts/`...), not the
minified `dist/` files - but import from the entry points, not from `src/`.

**Versions** follow semver from 1.0: everything on this page and in the types keeps working through
1.x, defaults included. Exact pixels and error wording can change; nothing is removed without a
release that warns first, naming the replacement. A warning that something is deprecated says what
to write instead - do that.

## Conventions

- **Coordinates**: right-handed, **+Y up**, +Z towards the viewer, units are metres.
- **Angles** are radians, except a perspective camera's `fov`, which is degrees.
- **Vectors in**: `[x, y, z]` arrays (objects `{ x, y, z }` also work). On objects, `position`,
  `rotation`, `scale` are small vector classes: `node.position.set(1, 2, 3)`, `node.rotation.y += 0.1`,
  `node.scale.x = 2` and `node.position = [1, 2, 3]` (copied in) all work.
- **Colours**: `'#ff8800'`, `'#f80'`, `0xff8800`, CSS names (`'orange'`), `'rgb(255 136 0)'`, or
  `[r, g, b]` 0-1. Inputs are sRGB.
- **Time** is seconds. Handlers get what they act on as an argument (arrow functions are fine).
- **The orbit**: `view.controls.spherical` is `{ yaw, pitch, distance }` about `camera.target` - yaw 0
  looks from +Z (the front), `Math.PI / 2` from +X (the right); pitch is above the horizon. Setting it
  moves the camera, within the limits. Move the camera or its target yourself at any time - the orbit
  turns about wherever they are; `camera.target = [x, y, z]` copies the point in.
- **One options object per constructor.** Unknown option names throw an error that says what to use
  instead - read it, it usually names the fix.

## The minimal app

```html
<canvas id="c" style="width: 100%; height: 100vh; display: block"></canvas>
<script type="module" src="./main.js"></script>
```

```js
import { View, Mesh, box, DirectionalLight } from 'phoria2'

const view = new View({ canvas: '#c', orbit: true, background: '#1c1c20' })
const cube = view.scene.add(new Mesh({ geometry: box(2), material: { color: 'orange' } }))
view.scene.add(new DirectionalLight({ direction: [-1, -2, -1] }))
view.start((dt) => cube.rotateY(0.6 * dt))
```

The canvas needs a size from CSS; the View matches its drawing buffer to it and follows resizes
itself. A scene with no lights is lit automatically (with a console note).

## View

```js
const view = new View({ canvas: '#c', orbit: true })
```

| Option | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `canvas` | a new full-window canvas | element or CSS selector |
| `camera` | `'perspective'`: a three-quarter view from the front right and above, fitted to the scene on the first frame | a preset - `'perspective'`, `'isometric'`, `'top'`, `'front'`, `'side'` (fitted to the scene on the first frame, unless you place or frame the camera first) - camera options (`{ position, target, fov }`), or a camera |
| `orbit` | `false` | `true`, or options: `{ autoRotate, inertia, minDistance, maxDistance, minPitch, maxPitch, pan, zoom, mode }`. `autoRotate`: `true` (a slow turn) or radians per second; it pauses while the user drags. `mode`: `'orbit'` (the default) or `'map'` - drags pan and the view never turns, for plans. `minDistance`/`maxDistance` limit zooming: the distance to the target, or for an orthographic camera the height of the view. Left-drag orbits, right-drag pans, wheel zooms |
| `background` | transparent | a colour |
| `highlight` | none | a colour mixed into whatever is under the pointer |
| `tooltip` | none | `(hit) => content` - see Interaction |
| `framing` | `'height'` | what stays in view as the canvas changes shape: `'height'`, `'width'`, or `'both'` (nothing framed is ever cut off - good for tiles). Also `{ keep, aspect }` |
| `renderMode` | `'auto'` | `'auto'` draws only when something changed (idle views cost nothing); `'always'`; `'manual'` |
| `toneMapping`, `exposure` | `'neutral'`, `1` | `'neutral'` \| `'aces'` \| `'none'`; also `view.toneMapping`, `view.exposure` |
| `bloom` | off | glow round bright parts (emissive, additive points and lines): `true` or `{ strength, radius, threshold }`; also `view.bloom` |
| `ambientOcclusion` | off | shading in the creases: `true` or `{ strength, radius }`; also `view.ambientOcclusion` - see Product viewer passes |
| `groundShadow` | off | a soft shadow on the ground under the solids, no light needed: `true` or `{ opacity, softness, height, y, size }`; also `view.groundShadow` |
| `fxaa` | `false` | smooth jagged edges with a pass over the finished picture; also `view.fxaa` |
| `autoLight` | `true` | light a scene that has no lights (a chart needs none of its own); `false` to leave it dark |
| `pixelRatio` | `min(devicePixelRatio, 2)` | |
| `context` | `'auto'` | WebGL context: own for the first four views on a page, then one shared context - so a page can hold any number of views |
| `keyboard` | `false` | `true` or `{ label: (hit) => text }`: use without a pointer, with a screen reader - see Interaction |
| `description` | none | what the view shows, for screen readers (the canvas's label); made from the scene when `keyboard` is on |
| `reducedMotion` | `'auto'` | as the system's reduced-motion setting: `frame()` jumps rather than glides, auto-rotation holds, charts change at once. `true` or `false` to choose |

Members: `view.scene`, `view.camera` (assign a camera or a preset name to switch), `view.controls`
(the orbit control), `view.renderer`, `view.width`, `view.height`, `view.description`, `view.reducedMotion`
(true or false as it stands - check it for motion of your own, such as a timeline; set `'auto'`, true or false).

Methods:

- `start(fn?)` - `fn(dt, t)` every frame. Time and node update handlers run anyway; you only need
  `start` for your own per-frame code.
- `frame(node?, { padding, direction, duration })` - move the camera so a node (default: the whole
  scene) fills the view, keeping the viewing direction - centred across, and a little below the
  middle so it stands rather than hangs. It fits what the camera draws - not hidden nodes, nor a
  chart's axis labels for the edges it isn't showing - so a chart fills the view. `padding` is the
  margin around it as a fraction of its size: `0` is a tight fit, `0.2` (the default) leaves a
  fifth, `0.5` half. `direction` looks from a preset's direction (`'perspective'`, `'top'`,
  `'front'`, `'side'`, `'isometric'` - the camera stays the kind it is) or a vector from the
  target towards the camera; `duration` (seconds) glides there - a press or the wheel stops it.
  A Reset button is `view.frame(undefined, { direction: 'perspective', duration: 0.6 })`; a guided
  tour flies from one node to the next with `view.frame(node, { duration: 1 })`.
- `on('click' | 'hover', (hit, event) => ...)` - see Interaction. Returns an unsubscribe function.
- `tooltip(fn)` - set the tooltip function later.
- `pick(x, y)` / `pick(event)` - the hit under a canvas position; `pickAll` for every hit.
- `pickArea(area)` - every hit inside a box `{ x, y, width, height }` or a lasso of `[x, y]` points
  (CSS pixels), nearest first - see Interaction.
- `rayAt(x, y)` / `rayAt(event)` - the world `Ray` through a canvas position, for placing things:
  `ray.at(ray.intersectPlane([0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 0]))` is the point on the floor under the pointer
  (`intersectPlane` returns null when the ray runs along the plane or away from it).
- `await view.toImage()` - a PNG `Blob` of the picture, labels included.
- `await view.explain()` - a plain-text report of what is drawn, with warnings ("nothing in view",
  "no lights", labels hidden...). Use it to debug a blank or wrong picture.
- `view.debug` (or the `debug` option) - pictures for a person checking a scene, drawn over it:
  `true` for all but normals, or `{ lights, shadows, bounds, normals, axes, camera, stats }`.
  - `lights`: an arrow for each directional light (over the scene's middle, the way it shines), a
    small sphere and a ring at its range for point lights, a cone for spot lights - in the light's colour.
  - `shadows`: the box (directional) or cone (spot) each shadow map is drawn from, in yellow - the
    usual reason a shadow is cut off, blocky or soft.
  - `bounds`: each drawable's world box, in cyan - what culling, `view.frame()` and shadow fitting
    see. `'hovered'`: only what is under the pointer (an instance's own box).
  - `normals`: a short magenta line along each vertex normal - for lighting that looks wrong on
    imported or generated geometry. Meshes up to 5,000 vertices when all are shown; `'hovered'` shows
    the mesh under the pointer, whatever its size.
  - `axes`: x, y and z at the origin, red, green and blue. `camera`: the point the orbit turns round.
  - `stats`: a corner readout - fps and frame time, the CPU time of a frame, draw calls, triangles,
    programs, textures and geometries; `true` is top left, or `'top-right'`, `'bottom-left'`,
    `'bottom-right'`.

  The helpers are lines in the scene's depth that also show faintly through what is in front of
  them. They aren't part of the scene: never picked, framed, saved or counted, and `explain()` says
  when debug drawing is on. Their code loads the first time debug is turned on.

  ```js
  view.debug = { lights: true, shadows: true, bounds: 'hovered', stats: 'bottom-right' }
  ```
- `render()`, `invalidate()` (redraw after changing data the view can't see), `dispose()`.

If a page shows nothing or the wrong thing, `console.log(await view.explain())` before anything else.
Errors thrown for bad options name the option and usually the fix.

## Changing things later

Everything can be changed after it is made, and the next frame shows it (the View redraws when
something changes):

- Nodes: `position`, `rotation`, `scale`, `visible`, `pickable`, `add`/`remove` children. `node.bounds`
  is always current - read it straight after adding or moving things.
- Materials: every property - `color.set(...)`, `opacity` (going below 1 makes it transparent;
  back to 1, opaque again), `emissive`, `roughness`, `width` on Lines, `size` on Points, maps.
- Instances: `setInstance`, `setColor`. Labels: `text`, `className`, `visible`.
- Lights: `intensity`, `color`, `direction`, `castShadow`. Scene: `background`, `environment`.
- View: `view.camera = 'top'` switches camera (a preset is fitted to the scene); `view.controls.mode`,
  `view.controls.autoRotate`, `view.controls.enabled`; `view.highlight`; `view.tooltip(fn)`.
- Charts: `chart.update(newRows)` or `chart.update({ color: 'other' })` - animated.

## Scene graph

Everything in a scene is a node. Node options (all optional): `name`, `position`, `rotation`
(Euler XYZ radians, `[x, y, z]`), `quaternion` (`[x, y, z, w]` or `{ x, y, z, w }`), `scale` (number or `[x, y, z]`), `visible`,
`pickable` (default true), `userData`, `children`, `onUpdate`, `clip` (a section plane - see
Cutaways), plus the interaction options below.

```js
const group = view.scene.add(new Group({ position: [0, 1, 0] }))   // add() returns what it added
group.add(new Mesh({ geometry: sphere(), material: { color: 'teal' } }))
node.onUpdate((node, dt, t) => { node.rotation.y += dt })
scene.find('lamp'); scene.findAll((n) => n.name.startsWith('rack')); scene.traverse((n) => {})
node.translate(x, y, z); node.rotateY(rad); node.lookAt([0, 0, 0])  // a camera with a target moves its target; a light shines there
node.remove(child); node.removeFromParent(); node.dispose()
node.bounds              // world-space Box3: .min, .max, .getCenter(), .getSize()
node.boundsFrom(camera)  // the same, for only what that camera draws (hidden and showFrom-off parts left out)
node.worldPosition       // read only
node.updateWorld()       // world matrices up to date now - ancestors, the node, everything under it -
                         // to read worldPosition or bounds after moving things, before the next frame
node.updateWorldTree()   // the same for the node and everything under it, when its parent is already current
```

**Cutaways**: `clip: { normal, offset, cap }` on any node cuts away everything in its subtree on the
`normal` side of a plane, `offset` along the normal from the node's origin, in the node's own space
(so it moves with the node). `cap` fills the cut faces of closed shapes with a colour, as a surface
lying on the plane - parts that touch join cleanly, and what is inside them stays hidden; without it
they show their hollow insides. Caps need closed solids: keep open surfaces (planes, open tubes) out
of a capped clip. The nearest clip above a mesh is the one that cuts it. Move the cut
by changing it in place: `engine.clip.offset = 0.5`. Cut-away parts cast no shadow and can't be
picked; points and lines aren't cut. A clip is one plane: there is no cutting out an octant or a
wedge - build the cut-open shape itself for that.

```js
const block = view.scene.add(new Group({ clip: { normal: [0, 0, 1], offset: 0, cap: '#c0392b' } }))
```

`Scene` (also `view.scene`) adds: `background` (colour, or a panorama texture), `environment`
(`'studio'` - built in, no download - `'none'`, or an `.hdr` url: image-based light for every lit
material), `environmentIntensity`, `backgroundBlur` (0-1, for a panorama background), `fog`.

**Fog**: `scene.fog = { color, density }` - exponential, thickening with distance like mist (try 0.02 -
0.1) - or `{ color, near, far }` for linear. Give `background` the same colour, so distant things melt
into it. Change it in place (`scene.fog.density = 0.08`); `null` turns it off. Additive glows fade
out with distance rather than turning fog-coloured; a material with `fog: false` (a sky dome, a far
backdrop) ignores it.

## Drawables

All drawables take `geometry`, `material`, `castShadow`, `receiveShadow`, `renderOrder` and `data`.

```js
new Mesh({ geometry: box(1), material: { color: '#c33', roughness: 0.3 } })
new Points({ geometry, material: { color: 'white', size: 4, sizeAttenuation: false } })  // size in pixels when not attenuated
new Lines({ geometry: edges(box(2)), material: { color: '#333', width: 2 } })            // segments: pairs of vertices; width in pixels
new Label({ text: 'Rack A1', position: [0, 2, 0], className: 'my-label', place: 'above' })
```

**Lines** dashed and with arrowheads - flow and direction in network diagrams. Dashes are material
options in the model's units: `dash` (0 is solid), `gap` (0 is the dash's length) and `dashOffset`,
which moves them along - animate it for traffic. Arrowheads are Lines options: `arrows: 'start' |
'end' | 'both'` puts them at the ends of each chain (segments each starting where the one before
ended - a polyline is one chain, separate links are one each), `arrowSize` in pixels (0, the default,
sizes them from the width). The dashes run on along a chain, and arrowheads are never dashed.

```js
const flow = view.scene.add(new Lines({ geometry: links, arrows: 'end', material: { color: '#4cc9f0', width: 2, dash: 0.3, gap: 0.15 } }))
view.start((dt) => { flow.material.dashOffset += dt * 0.8 })   // traffic moving along each link
```

**Points** each their own size, opacity or angle: give the geometry `sizes` (multiples of the material's
`size`), `opacities` (0-1) or `angles` (radians, turning the point's `map`), one per vertex. Such points
are drawn as camera-facing squares, so any size works and they stay whole at the edge of the view.
`sort: true` draws them furthest first each frame - for soft points with `blending: 'normal'`
(smoke, cloud) that would otherwise layer wrongly; with additive blending order doesn't matter.

**InstancedMesh** - many copies of one geometry in one draw call, for bars, racks, nodes:

```js
const bars = view.scene.add(new InstancedMesh({ geometry: box(1), material: { roughness: 0.5 }, data: rows }))  // count = rows.length
rows.forEach((r, i) => bars.setInstance(i, { position: [r.x, r.h / 2, r.z], scale: [0.8, r.h, 0.8], color: r.color }))
bars.setColor(3, 'red')
```

`setInstance(i, { position, rotation, quaternion, scale, color })`. An instance's `color` multiplies the
material's colour, which is white unless you set one - so the instance colour shows as given. `count` defaults to the number
of rows in `data`. For very large data, write `bars.instanceMatrices` (16 numbers per instance,
column-major) directly and call `bars.needsUpdate()`. An instance scaled to 0 is hidden: it draws
nothing, and bounds, framing, shadows and labels leave it out - so a pool can keep spare instances.
Positions and quaternions also take `{ x, y, z }` and `{ x, y, z, w }`, as physics engines return
them, so a physics bridge is one line a body:
`bricks.setInstance(i, { position: body.translation(), quaternion: body.rotation() })`.

**Labels** are HTML elements pinned to 3D points (style them with CSS). Options: `text`, `position`,
`className`, `place` (`'center'` | `'above'` | `'below'` | `'left'` | `'right'`), `offset` ([x, y]
pixels), `priority` (higher wins when labels overlap), `overlap` (`'hide'` | `'dim'` | `'show'` - what
a label does when covered), `occlude` (true: counts as covered when geometry is in front), `leader`
(true: a line from the point to the label, with a dot on the point - for callouts), `edge` (`'left'` |
`'right'`: set the label at that edge of the view, level with its point - callouts in a column, with
`leader: true`; `offset` then moves it in and up or down), `minScale` (show it only when zoomed in this
far - below).

A label answers the pointer when it has handlers: a Label with its own `onClick` or `onHover` is
clicked and hovered like a mesh (`new Label({ text: 'Mantle', onClick: () => show('mantle') })` - a
callout that opens its layer), and a label of an instance or point is part of it - clicking it is
clicking that bar, with the same hit. Other labels let the pointer through to the scene.

A Label can show an element of your own instead of text - `content` takes any element: an equation
typeset by KaTeX or MathJax, an icon, a badge. It's placed, given way to, dimmed and clicked like any
label, and a change of `content` (or of its size - KaTeX's fonts arriving) redraws. `text` is optional
then, and stands in for the element where one can't go: `view.toImage()` paints the text (a canvas
can't draw HTML; with no text the label is left out of the image), and `toJSON()` keeps the text.

```js
import katex from 'katex'
const formula = document.createElement('span')
katex.render('y = \\sin(a x)\\cos(z)', formula)
view.scene.add(new Label({ content: formula, text: 'y = sin(ax) cos(z)', position: [0, 2.5, 0] }))
```

**Labels per instance or point**, without a Label node each:

```js
new InstancedMesh({ geometry: box(1), data: rows, labels: { text: (row) => row.name, place: 'above', priority: (row) => row.alert ? 2 : 0 } })
```

**Labels by zoom level**: `minScale` on any label shows it only when the view is zoomed in at least that
far - that many CSS pixels to one world unit, at the label's point (perspective or orthographic alike).
Until then it takes no part in the layout, so it can't push other labels out. `labels` can also be a
list, several labels per instance - the short one always, the details as you come closer:

```js
new InstancedMesh({ geometry: box(1), data: elements, labels: [
  { text: (e) => e.symbol, place: 'center', className: 'symbol' },
  { text: (e) => e.name, place: 'below', className: 'name', minScale: 45 },
] })
```

Pick `minScale` by looking: at the zoom where the details should appear, a world unit spans that many
pixels (a 1-unit tile drawn 60 px wide is 60). `view.explain()` counts the labels still waiting.

## Geometry

Generators return a `Geometry`; each takes one options object (a number is the main size):

| | Options |
|---|---|
| `box(size \| { width, height, depth })` | centred on the origin |
| `sphere({ radius, segments, rings })` | |
| `plane(size \| { width, depth })` | in the x-z plane, facing up (+Y) |
| `cylinder({ radius, radiusTop, height, segments })` | along Y, centred; `radiusTop: 0` is a cone, its tip at the + end of the axis (up) |
| `torus({ radius, tube })`, `icosphere({ radius, detail })` | |
| `lathe({ points, segments, axis })` | a profile of `[radius, y]` pairs, bottom up, turned about Y - pistons, bottles, bolts (listed top down, it faces inward) |
| `extrude({ shape, holes, depth, axis })` | an outline of `[x, y]` pairs (and hole outlines) pushed along Z, centred - plates, brackets, logos |
| `grid({ size, divisions })` | floor grid, for `Lines` |
| `edges(geometry, { angle })` | the edges of any geometry, for `Lines`: where faces turn more than `angle` degrees (default 1) - 30 keeps round surfaces clean, outlining a part as a drawing does |

`axis: 'x' | 'y' | 'z'` lays `cylinder`, `lathe` and `extrude` along another axis - no rotating the mesh
to suit. An extruded outline is drawn as seen from the axis's + end, centred along the axis: with
`'y'`, from above - the outline's x is the world's x and its y runs towards -z, away from the front.

**Outlines** for `extrude` and `lathe` - lists of `[x, y]` points, anticlockwise, to spread together or
cut as holes: `outline.circle(radius | { radius, segments, center })`, `outline.rect({ width, height,
radius, center })` (`radius` rounds the corners), `outline.polygon({ radius, sides, angle })`,
`outline.arc({ radius, from, to, center })` (angles in radians from +x; both ends included, for joining
into a shape), `outline.gear({ radius, teeth, depth })`.

```js
// a connecting rod: two eyes joined by their sides, each bored through, lying across x
extrude({
  shape: [...outline.arc({ radius: 0.15, from: -0.4, to: Math.PI + 0.4, center: [0, 1.4] }), ...outline.arc({ radius: 0.3, from: Math.PI - 0.4, to: 2 * Math.PI + 0.4 })],
  holes: [outline.circle(0.2), outline.circle({ radius: 0.09, center: [0, 1.4] })],
  depth: 0.16, axis: 'x',
})
```

Your own: `new Geometry({ positions, normals?, uvs?, uvs2?, colors?, indices? })` - flat arrays, xyz per
vertex; `colors` are rgb 0-1 per vertex (use `material: { vertexColors: true }`); `uvs2` is a second UV
set, for baked occlusion and light maps (below). To animate one - cloth, a wave, a morph - write
`geometry.positions` in place and call `geometry.needsUpdate()` each frame; normals you didn't give are
worked out again to follow the shape.

## Materials

One material type, given as a plain object:

```js
{ color: 'white' }                                   // lit, physically based
{ color: '#c33', roughness: 0.2, metalness: 1 }      // metal
{ color: 'orange', unlit: true }                     // flat colour, ignores lights
{ color: '#8cf', opacity: 0.4 }                      // transparent: fades the whole surface
{ transmission: 1, roughness: 0.05 }                 // clear glass
{ color: '#a3121f', metalness: 0.6, clearcoat: 1 }   // car paint: a glossy coat over it
{ color: '#1f2d6e', roughness: 0.9, sheen: 1 }       // velvet: cloth's bright rim
{ color: '#111', roughness: 0.1, iridescence: 1 }   // oil on water: a thin film's shifting colours
{ color: '#ccc', metalness: 1, anisotropy: 0.8 }     // brushed metal
{ color: '#f2e4c4', translucency: 0.8 }              // paper: lit from behind too
{ matcap: 'clay.png' }                               // the look from a picture of a lit sphere
{ color: '#e4572e', toon: 3 }                        // cartoon: three flat tones
{ emissive: '#ff0', emissiveIntensity: 3 }           // glows
{ map: 'wood.jpg', normalMap: 'wood_n.png' }         // textures from urls
```

**Exact colour**: an `unlit` material draws exactly the colour it is given - `'#e15759'` is
`#e15759` on screen and in `toImage()`, whatever the tone mapping - and so do instance colours,
vertex colours, colour maps, lines and points. Use it for swatches, legends, status colours and
brand colours. A lit surface doesn't keep its colour: light and tone mapping are meant to change
it. Vertex colours blend across each face in linear light, so a ramp between two vertices differs
slightly from a 2D tool's; subdivide for a closer match.

Properties: `color`, `opacity`, `roughness` (0.5), `metalness` (0), `emissive`,
`emissiveIntensity`, `unlit`, `flatShading`, `doubleSided`, `vertexColors`, `fog` (true), `blending`
(`'normal'`, `'additive'` - adds light, for glows and sparks - or `'multiply'` - darkens what is behind, as a colour
filter does: cyan over magenta is blue), `alphaTest` (cut-outs: drop pixels with less alpha - leaves, fences),
`map`, `normalMap`/`normalScale`, `bumpMap`/`bumpScale`, `roughnessMap`, `metalnessMap`, `aoMap`,
`emissiveMap`, `lightMap`/`lightMapIntensity`, `environmentIntensity` (1), `transmission`, `clearcoat`/`clearcoatRoughness`, `sheen`/`sheenColor`/`sheenRoughness`, `iridescence`/`iridescenceIor`/`iridescenceThickness`/`iridescenceThicknessMin`/`iridescenceThicknessMap`, `ior`/
`specularIntensity`/`specularColor`, `anisotropy`/`anisotropyRotation`, `translucency`/`translucencyColor`, `matcap`, `toon` (below); `size`/`sizeAttenuation` for Points, `width` for Lines. Change later through
`mesh.material.color.set('#0f0')`, `mesh.material.opacity = 0.5`, or a whole new one: `mesh.material = { color: 'red' }`
(options become a Material, as in the constructor; `mesh.geometry = box(2)` likewise).

A **bump map** is a height texture (red channel) shown as bumps - no normal map to make, so it suits
heights drawn in code. `bumpScale` is how high a height of 1 stands, in the mesh's units. Textures
take `anisotropy` (default 8, up to the GPU's limit, 1 for off), which keeps floors and roads sharp
into the distance. A cut-out (`alphaTest`) is what is left of it everywhere: its shadow, its outline, ambient
occlusion, and picking - hover, click and tooltips go through its holes to what is behind (picked on
the GPU, which reads the texture). `pickAll`, `pickArea` and `Raycaster` see only geometry, so to them a
cut-out is its whole shape. A Texture given to a
data map (`normalMap`, `bumpMap`, `roughnessMap`, `metalnessMap`, `aoMap`) is read as data, not colour,
unless its `colorSpace` was set on purpose - `normalMap: await loadTexture('n.png')` just works.

**Canvas and video textures**: a texture's `image` can be a canvas - draw on it, then call
`texture.needsUpdate()` - or a `<video>`, whose frames upload by themselves while it plays, with
nothing to call. For a big canvas drawn on a little at a time (paint, a map being revealed), say what
changed - `texture.needsUpdate({ x, y, width, height })`, in the canvas's pixels from its top left -
and only that rectangle is sent, rather than the whole canvas every frame (several calls before a
frame add up). `new Texture({ url: 'promo.mp4' })` (or .webm, .ogv, .mov, .m4v) makes the video
for you, muted and looping so browsers let it start by itself; `texture.image` is that `<video>` -
pause, seek or unmute it as any other. A browser that blocks autoplay leaves it on its first frame
until `texture.image.play()` from a click. Video textures make no mipmaps (they would be remade
every frame) unless `mipmaps: true`. Put one on an unlit plane for a screen:
`{ map: new Texture({ url: 'promo.mp4', wrap: 'clamp' }), unlit: true }`.

**Render textures** - what a camera sees, as a map: a camera feed on a monitor, a minimap on a
panel, a product from a second angle beside it.

```js
const cctv = scene.add(new PerspectiveCamera({ position: [8, 4, 6], target: [0, 0, 0], fov: 60 }))
const feed = new RenderTexture({ camera: cctv, width: 512, height: 320 })
scene.add(new Mesh({ geometry: plane({ width: 3.2, depth: 2 }), rotation: [Math.PI / 2, 0, 0], material: { map: feed, unlit: true } }))
```

- A `RenderTexture` is a Texture, so it goes in any map slot. Give it a camera of its own - placed in
  the scene, or a child of something that moves (a camera riding on a robot goes where it goes). The
  camera's aspect follows `width / height`.
- The view showing it draws it first, before each frame: `update: 'frame'` (the default) each frame
  the view draws, `update: n` every nth (a map needn't be drawn as often), `'manual'` once and then
  after each `feed.needsUpdate()`. A view only draws when something changed - moving the texture's
  camera counts.
- It draws the view's scene, or `scene` for another. Plainly: lights, shadows, fog and background,
  none of the view's effects (bloom, ambient occlusion, ground shadow, FXAA), no labels. Whatever
  shows the texture is left out of it, so a monitor never films itself.
- Its colours are the main view's, read the right way up. `mipmaps` (default true) keeps it smooth
  seen small or at an angle; `wrap` defaults to 'clamp'. `renderer.info.renderTextures` and
  `view.explain()` say how many were drawn. It can't be saved with `toJSON()` (its camera is a live
  object). `feed.dispose()` frees it.

**Placing a texture**: `repeat` ([u, v] times across), `offset`, and `rotation` (radians, about
`center`: [0, 0], the corner, by default - [0.5, 0.5] for the middle) - applied in that order, as glTF's
`KHR_texture_transform` does, and each map keeps its own: a fabric's colour can repeat 7 times while
its normal map repeats twice. Animate them to scroll or spin a pattern.

**Baked occlusion and light maps**: occlusion and lighting baked in Blender, Unreal or Unity need
every surface on its own patch of texture, so they come on a second UV set while the first tiles
colour and detail. Give the geometry `uvs2` and the texture `uvSet: 1` - glTF models do both
for you (`TEXCOORD_1`, `texCoord: 1`). Read through the first set, baked occlusion lands in the
wrong places as dark smudges. `lightMap` is light baked into a texture, added as light from all
round (`lightMapIntensity`, 1) - the soft, cheap lighting of architectural scenes.

**Environment strength per material**: `environmentIntensity` (1) scales how much of the
scene's environment - its light and its reflections - one material takes: lower for a matte floor in
a shiny showroom, higher to make one product catch the light, without changing the scene's.

**Glass**: `transmission` (0-1) lets light through as glass does. Unlike `opacity`, which fades
everything - reflections too, so faded things look washed out, as dimmed chart bars should - glass
keeps its reflections whole, and shows less of what is behind it towards its edges, where it
reflects nearly everything. Its colour shows in proportion to `1 - transmission`: `transmission: 0.6`
with a colour is tinted glass. Keep `roughness` low for clear glass, higher for frosted. There is
no refraction - what is behind isn't bent. It shines with an `environment` to reflect
(`'studio'`, or better an `.hdr`).

**Clearcoat**: `clearcoat` (0-1) puts a clear glossy layer over the surface - car paint, lacquered
wood, varnish - with its own sharp reflection over the base's softer one; `clearcoatRoughness` (0,
a mirror) makes it satin. Normal and bump maps show under a smooth coat.

**Sheen**: `sheen` (0-1) is the soft bright rim of cloth at grazing angles - velvet, felt,
upholstery - which plain roughness can't give: without it fabric looks like matte plastic.
`sheenColor` (white) tints it, often lighter than the cloth or another colour entirely;
`sheenRoughness` (0.5) runs from a thin bright rim (0) to a broad soft glow (1).

**Iridescence**: `iridescence` (0-1) lays a thin film over the surface whose colours shift with
the angle it is seen at - soap bubbles, oil on water, beetle shells, anodised metal, dichroic
glass. It works on any material: over `transmission` it is a bubble, over a dark base an oil
slick, over `metalness: 1` anodised titanium. `iridescenceThickness` (400) is the film's thickness
in nanometres - about 200-800 shows colours, and changing it changes which; `iridescenceIor` (1.3)
is the film's index of refraction (soap 1.33). For bands across the surface, as a bubble's swirl,
give `iridescenceThicknessMap`: its green channel runs the thickness from `iridescenceThicknessMin`
(100) at 0 to `iridescenceThickness` at 1.

**Reflectance**: `ior` (1.5) sets how strongly a non-metal reflects - water 1.33, glass and plastic
1.5, diamond 2.4 - and glass with `transmission` reflects more the higher it is.
`specularIntensity` (1) scales a non-metal's reflections, 0 for none (chalk, clay, unglazed
pottery); `specularColor` tints them face on. Metals take their reflections from `color`, so
these leave them alone.

**Brushed metal**: `anisotropy` (0-1) - the material's, not a texture's filtering - draws highlights and reflections out along the brushing -
brushed aluminium, steel appliances, the bottom of a pan. The brushing runs along the UVs' u (round
a sphere or cylinder, say; round the up axis on a mesh with no UVs); `anisotropyRotation`
(radians) turns it - `Math.PI / 2` runs it along v. Use it with `metalness: 1` and a middling
`roughness` (0.2-0.4).

**Translucency**: `translucency` (0-1) lets light through thin surfaces, so they are lit from
behind as well as in front - leaves against the sun, paper lanterns and lampshades with a light
inside, curtains. What passes through is taken from what is scattered back, so at 1 a surface is lit
only through it. `translucencyColor` (white) tints the light that comes through. It is light
through a thin sheet, not light scattering inside a solid: a lantern glows, marble stays marble.

**Matcap**: `matcap` is a picture of a lit sphere - clay, wax, chrome, a painted ball - that gives the
whole look: each point takes the colour from where a sphere facing the same way would show it. It is
the clay look of sculpting tools and CAD viewers, good for reading a model's shape, and costs one
texture lookup - no lights, shadows or environment, which it ignores. Its shine stays put as the camera
turns, since the light is in the picture, so it looks out of place beside lit things. `color` and
`map` multiply it, so one grey matcap serves any colour; normal and bump maps and `flatShading`
still shape it. Any matcap image works, or draw one on a canvas (`new Texture({ image: canvas })`).

**Toon**: `toon: 3` shades in that many flat tones (2 or more; 0, the default, is smooth), with one
hard-edged highlight - a cartoon. Lights and shadows work as usual; the shaded tone is the scene's
ambient and hemisphere light, so add some for a lighter shade. Metals keep their colour, with a
highlight of it. Pair it with `outline` on the nodes for inked edges.

glTF models bring glass, clearcoat, sheen, reflectance, brushed metal and translucency from `KHR_materials_transmission`, `KHR_materials_clearcoat`,
`KHR_materials_sheen`, `KHR_materials_ior`, `KHR_materials_specular`, `KHR_materials_anisotropy`
and `KHR_materials_diffuse_transmission` (by their factors; their textures aren't read), and
iridescence from `KHR_materials_iridescence` (its thickness texture too).

**Models without UVs** (scans, CAD exports) can still take maps: `triplanar: 40` projects them
from the mesh's three axes instead of using UVs, repeating 40 times per unit of the mesh's own space.
The maps stay on the mesh as it moves; normal maps follow the surface; a map's `repeat` and `offset` apply
on top, as with UVs (animate `offset` to scroll a pattern). 0 (the default) uses the UVs.

```js
{ bumpMap: pores, bumpScale: 0.0005, roughnessMap: sheen, triplanar: 45 }   // bone texture on a scanned skull
```

**Shader hooks** - a few lines of GLSL of your own, run at fixed points inside phoria2's shader, for
what the material options can't say: waves, wind, dissolves, scanlines, glows, colour by height. You
write statements, not a shader: lighting, shadows, fog, clipping, picking and outlines keep working -
a waving flag casts a waving shadow and is picked where it is drawn. Meshes, instanced meshes, points
and lines all take them, as `material.shader`:

```js
new Mesh({ geometry: plane({ width: 3, depth: 2, segments: 40 }), material: {
  color: '#3a7bd5', doubleSided: true,
  shader: {
    uniforms: { uAmp: 0.25 },
    vertex: 'local.y += sin(local.x * 3.0 + uTime * 3.0) * uAmp;',        // a wave, in the geometry's own space
    fragment: 'base.rgb *= 0.8 + 0.2 * sin(vWorldPosition.y * 20.0);',   // stripes, before lighting
    lit: 'color += vec3(0.0, 0.1, 0.2) * (0.5 + 0.5 * sin(uTime));',     // a glow the light doesn't touch
  },
} })
```

Three hooks, each optional. What each can use (✎ = change it; everything else is read only):

| | Mesh / InstancedMesh | Points | Lines |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vertex` - each vertex, before it is placed | ✎ `local` (vec3, own space), ✎ `n` (vec3 normal), `uv` (vec2), `index` (int: the instance) | ✎ `local`, ✎ `size` (float, times the material's), `index` (int: the point) | ✎ `local`, `along` (float: 0 at a segment's start, 1 at its end), `index` (int: the segment) - runs once per end, so a segment moves but stays straight |
| `fragment` - each pixel, before lighting | ✎ `base` (vec4: linear colour, alpha), ✎ `emissive` (vec3), ✎ `normal` (vec3: the shading normal, world space, facing the viewer - bend it for relief lit per pixel), `vUv`, `vWorldPosition`, `vNormal`, `vColor`; `discard` | ✎ `base`, `pointUv` (vec2, 0-1 across the point), `index` (int); `discard` | ✎ `base`, `distance` (float: along the line, in the geometry's units), `index` (int: the segment); `discard` |
| `lit` - each pixel, after lighting | ✎ `color` (vec3, linear, lit), ✎ `base.a` | ✎ `color`, ✎ `base.a` | ✎ `color`, ✎ `base.a` |

Every hook can also read `uTime` - the View's clock in seconds - and the uniforms you give, and
call functions for randomness and texture without a texture (hooks can't define their own). `p`
is a vec2 or vec3, and every result is 0 to 1:

- `hash(x)` - from a float, vec2 or vec3's exact bits. The same on every GPU for the same bits, so hash
  exact things - `hash(float(index))` gives each point, instance or segment its own random number,
  `hash(floor(vUv * 20.0))` each cell of a grid. An interpolated value such as `vWorldPosition` can
  differ in its last bits from GPU to GPU, and so can its hash.
- `vnoise(p)` - value noise: random values at whole-number points, eased between. Cheapest; looks
  blockier, its features lined up with the axes.
- `snoise(p)` - simplex noise: smoother, rounder, no grid to see - the better choice for anything
  natural. About one feature per unit of `p`: scale `p` up for finer detail, `snoise(vUv * 10.0)`,
  `snoise(vec3(local.xz, uTime))` to change over time.
- `snoised(p)` - simplex noise with its gradient: a vec3 (value, d/dx, d/dy) from a vec2, a vec4
  from a vec3. The slope for a normal, with no extra samples.
- `vfbm(p)`, `sfbm(p)` - fractal noise: octaves of value or simplex noise added up, each finer and
  half as strong, each turned so their grids don't line up. Five octaves; `sfbm(p, 8)` for more
  detail, fewer for softer and cheaper (1-12). Mostly 0.25-0.75 - the octaves average out.
- `sfbmd(p)`, `sfbmd(p, octaves)` - simplex fbm with its gradient, as `snoised`: terrain normals.
- `voronoi(p)` - cellular (Worley) noise: a random point in each unit cell of `p`. Returns a vec3 -
  `x` the distance to the nearest point (F1), `y` to the second nearest (F2), both in cells, and `z` a
  random 0-1 for the nearest point's cell. `y - x` is 0 on the edges between cells: cracks, cells,
  scales, stone, crystals; `z` gives each cell its own colour or height. A vec3 `p` with time as one
  axis makes the cells drift and re-form. Costs 9 cells (vec2) or 27 (vec3) - more than `snoise`.

And the everyday ones, with `cameraPosition` (vec3, the camera in world space) to read too:

- `srgb(c)` - a colour as picked (sRGB, as in a colour picker or CSS) to the linear colour hooks work
  in: `base.rgb = srgb(vec3(0.75, 0.12, 0.16))` is the red you picked, not a pale pink.
- `hsv2rgb(h, s, v)` (or a vec3) - hue, saturation and value 0-1 to a linear colour. Hue 0 red, 1/3
  green, 2/3 blue, wrapping: `hsv2rgb(fract(vWorldPosition.y * 0.2 - uTime * 0.1), 0.8, 1.0)`.
- `palette(t, a, b, c, d)` - Inigo Quilez's cosine palette, `a + b cos(2pi(c t + d))`, its four
  vec3s as picked, the result linear. `palette(t, vec3(0.5), vec3(0.5), vec3(1.0), vec3(0.0, 0.33,
  0.67))` is a rainbow; other a-d give heat, ocean, pastel ramps.
- `fresnel(normal, position, power)` - how side-on a surface is to the camera, 0 facing it, 1 edge-on,
  sharpened by the power: rim light, holograms, force fields, `fresnel(vNormal, vWorldPosition, 3.0)`.
- `rotate2(angle)` - a mat2 turning anticlockwise: `rotate2(a) * v`. `rotate3(axis, angle)` - a mat3
  turning about an axis. Twists, spins, turned uvs or noise.
- `remap(x, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax)` - from one range to another (not clamped; float, vec2 or
  vec3 x). `saturate(x)` - clamped to 0-1, as HLSL has it.

- **`uniforms`**, by GLSL name: a number (float), two to four numbers (vec2-vec4), a colour string or
  Color (vec3, sent linear) or a Texture (sampler2D, read with `texture(uName, uv)`). Change one on
  `material.shader.uniforms` (`mesh.material.shader.uniforms.uAmp = 0.5`) and the View redraws; assign
  a new `material.shader` to change the code. Names starting `gl_` or `phoria`, `uTime`, and phoria2's
  own uniforms (`uColor`, `uModel`, `uOpacity`...) are taken.
- **`uTime`**: a hook that reads it keeps the View drawing while time runs - no frame loop of your own.
  `view.stop()` freezes it.
- **Every pass runs the vertex hook** - shadow maps, outlines, GPU picking. A mesh's `fragment`
  `discard` cuts its shadow and its picking too, so a dissolve leaves no shadow of what has gone.
- **`bounds`**: how far, in world units, the vertex hook can move a vertex. Bounds are padded by it for
  culling, `view.frame()` and shadows; without it a vertex hook turns frustum culling off for the node.
- **Picking** a node a vertex hook moves is always done on the GPU, so clicks, hovers and tooltips find
  it where it is drawn (the hit has the point, not a normal or uv). `pickAll`, `pickArea` and
  `Raycaster` work from the geometry as given, not as moved.
- **A hook that doesn't compile** is reported once, by its own line numbers - `shader.vertex line 2:
  'wobble' : undeclared identifier` - with the names it can use, and the material is drawn without its
  hooks. `view.explain()` lists the hooked materials.

Recipes - each a material option to copy:

```js
// bumps lit per pixel from any height: bend the shading normal by its slope - crisp at any mesh
// resolution, no vertices moved (here a surface facing up, its uvs along x and z)
shader: { fragment: `
  vec2 q = vUv * 20.0;
  float e = 0.01, h = sfbm(q, 4);
  vec2 slope = vec2(sfbm(q + vec2(e, 0.0), 4) - h, sfbm(q + vec2(0.0, e), 4) - h) / e;
  normal = normalize(normal - vec3(slope.x, 0.0, slope.y) * 0.05);` }

// a wave with its normal bent to match, so the light follows the folds (a plane, a flag, a sheet)
shader: { uniforms: { uAmp: 0.2 }, vertex: `
  float phase = local.x * 3.0 - uTime * 4.0;
  local.y += sin(phase) * uAmp;
  n = normalize(vec3(-cos(phase) * 3.0 * uAmp, 1.0, 0.0));` }

// ripples spreading from the middle of a plane (give it segments: 64 or so)
shader: { vertex: `
  float r = length(local.xz), phase = r * 6.0 - uTime * 3.0, h = 0.04 * exp(-r * 0.4);
  local.y += sin(phase) * h;
  vec2 slope = local.xz / max(r, 1e-3) * cos(phase) * 6.0 * h;
  n = normalize(vec3(-slope.x, 1.0, -slope.y));` }

// breathing: grow and shrink about the middle
shader: { vertex: 'local *= 1.0 + 0.06 * sin(uTime * 2.0);' }

// dissolve through fractal noise, its edge glowing (its shadow dissolves too)
shader: { fragment: `
  float level = 0.5 - 0.55 * cos(uTime * 0.6);
  float v = sfbm(vUv * vec2(10.0, 3.0));
  if (v < level) discard;
  emissive += vec3(1.0, 0.2, 0.02) * smoothstep(level + 0.05, level, v) * 5.0;` }

// terrain from simplex fbm, its normal from the same call's gradient (a plane with segments: 128
// or so); the octaves set how rugged - 3 rolling hills, 8 craggy
shader: { uniforms: { uOctaves: 7 }, vertex: `
  vec3 h = sfbmd(local.xz * 0.4, int(uOctaves));
  local.y += h.x * 2.0;
  n = normalize(vec3(-h.y * 2.0 * 0.4, 1.0, -h.z * 2.0 * 0.4));` }

// a texture uniform: scroll a noise or pattern image across a surface
shader: { uniforms: { uPattern: patternTexture }, fragment: 'base.rgb *= texture(uPattern, vUv * 4.0 + vec2(uTime * 0.1, 0.0)).rgb;' }

// colour by height - a ramp from deep blue at y = 0 to orange at y = 2
shader: { fragment: 'base.rgb = mix(vec3(0.01, 0.05, 0.5), vec3(1.0, 0.25, 0.0), clamp(vWorldPosition.y / 2.0, 0.0, 1.0));' }

// rim glow: a hologram or force field - a faint body, bright where it turns away (with
// transparent: true)
shader: {
  fragment: 'base.rgb = srgb(vec3(0.25, 0.9, 1.0)) * 0.15; emissive += srgb(vec3(0.25, 0.9, 1.0)) * fresnel(vNormal, vWorldPosition, 2.5) * 2.0;',
  lit: 'base.a *= 0.3 + 0.7 * fresnel(vNormal, vWorldPosition, 1.5);',
}

// a twist: each height turned further round the y axis, its normal turned with it (give the mesh segments)
shader: { vertex: 'mat2 turn = rotate2(local.y * 1.2 * sin(uTime)); local.xz = turn * local.xz; n.xz = turn * n.xz;' }

// a hue climbing an object, and a cosine palette across another
shader: { fragment: 'base.rgb = hsv2rgb(fract(vWorldPosition.y * 0.2 - uTime * 0.1), 0.75, 1.0);' }
shader: { fragment: 'base.rgb = palette(vUv.x + uTime * 0.05, vec3(0.5), vec3(0.5), vec3(1.0), vec3(0.0, 0.33, 0.67));' }

// instances as a meter: each bar's height from one sine, a phase apart by index, remapped and saturated
shader: { vertex: 'float h = saturate(remap(sin(uTime * 2.0 + float(index) * 0.5), -1.0, 1.0, 0.05, 1.0)); local.y = (local.y + 0.5) * h - 0.5;' }

// cracked lava: dark crust plates, each its own shade, molten in the cracks between them (time as
// the third axis, so the plates drift and re-form)
shader: { fragment: `
  vec3 v = voronoi(vec3(vUv * 8.0, uTime * 0.2));
  float crack = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 0.12, v.y - v.x);
  base.rgb = srgb(vec3(0.16, 0.12, 0.11)) * (0.5 + 0.9 * v.z);
  emissive += vec3(1.0, 0.25, 0.0) * crack * 4.0;` }

// stained glass: each cell a random hue, dark leading between them
shader: { fragment: 'vec3 v = voronoi(vUv * 6.0); base.rgb = hsv2rgb(v.z, 0.7, 1.0) * smoothstep(0.02, 0.06, v.y - v.x);' }

// scanlines over the lit picture
shader: { lit: 'color *= 0.75 + 0.25 * step(0.5, fract(vWorldPosition.y * 20.0 - uTime));' }

// fade with distance from a point (with transparent: true on the material)
shader: { uniforms: { uCentre: [0, 0, 0] }, lit: 'base.a *= 1.0 - smoothstep(2.0, 4.0, distance(vWorldPosition, uCentre));' }

// points: twinkling, each at its own rate, and soft and round
shader: {
  vertex: 'size *= 1.0 + 0.6 * sin(uTime * (1.5 + hash(float(index)) * 3.0) + float(index));',
  fragment: 'base.a *= smoothstep(1.0, 0.0, length(pointUv * 2.0 - 1.0));',
}

// lines: pulses running along them (distance is along each run of joined segments), each line's
// at its own time
shader: { fragment: 'base.rgb += vec3(0.3, 0.9, 1.0) * smoothstep(0.85, 1.0, fract(distance * 0.6 - uTime + hash(float(index)))) * 4.0;' }
```

Mistakes to avoid:

- **Colours are linear**, as the shader works, so an sRGB-looking value comes out pale. Wrap a colour
  as picked in `srgb()` - `srgb(vec3(0.75, 0.12, 0.16))` - or write linear values, roughly the sRGB
  value squared: orange `vec3(1.0, 0.22, 0.0)`. `hsv2rgb` and `palette` give linear colour already,
  and colour uniforms given as strings are converted for you.
- **Hooks are statements**, run inside phoria2's `main()`: no functions of your own, no `uniform`
  declarations (use `uniforms`), no `return` in a mesh or points hook. Declare locals as you like.
  `hash`, the noises and the fbms are there for what you'd otherwise write a function for.
- **Randomness from `hash()`, not `fract(sin(x) * 43758.5453)`**: the sin trick multiplies a GPU's
  last bits of `sin` into the answer, so the same scene comes out differently on different GPUs.
  `hash` is integer arithmetic, exact everywhere.
- **`index` is an int**: `float(index)` to do sums with it.
- **Bend the normal when you move vertices**, or the light shades the shape as it was: change `n`
  (meshes) to match, and keep it normalised. Waves on a flat plane need `segments` to bend at all.
- **Fine relief belongs in the fragment hook**: moving vertices can only be as sharp as the mesh's
  resolution - a steep step (cracks, tiles, grooves) becomes a staircase between them. Bend `normal`
  in the fragment hook instead, lit per pixel, and keep any vertex movement gentle.
- **Fades need `transparent: true`**: changing `base.a` in an opaque material changes nothing.
  `discard` works either way.
- **Move in the geometry's own space**: `local` is before the node's position, rotation and scale (and
  an instance's), so a wave along `local.y` turns with the mesh.
- **Use `vWorldPosition`** for effects fixed in the world - a band at a height, a fade round a point -
  and `vUv` for ones fixed to the surface.
- **Lines move by their ends**: a straight segment stays straight - give the geometry more segments to
  bend a line.

## Lights and cameras

| | Options |
|---|---|
| `AmbientLight` | `color`, `intensity` |
| `HemisphereLight` | `sky`, `ground`, `intensity` |
| `DirectionalLight` | `color`, `intensity`, `direction` (the way it travels, e.g. `[-1, -2, -1]`), `castShadow`, `shadowBounds` |
| `PointLight` | `color`, `intensity`, `position`, `range` - inverse-square falloff, so intensity ~ distance squared (30 lights things ~5 m away); `castShadow` |
| `SpotLight` | point light options plus `direction`, `angle`, `penumbra`, `castShadow` |

Intensity 1 on a directional light lights a white surface facing it to white.

**Light limits**: a scene draws at most 2 directional lights and 4 point and spot lights together -
the first found in scene order; hidden ones don't count. Any more are ignored, with a console warning,
so a fifth lamp simply doesn't light anything. For a room of lamps, light it broadly with
`scene.environment` or a `HemisphereLight` (no limit), use real lights for the few that matter most -
near the camera, or casting shadows - and give the rest emissive materials so they still glow.
Toggle `visible` to move the real lights to where the action is.

**Shadows**: one directional light, up to four spot lights and one point light with `castShadow: true`;
meshes opt in with `castShadow` and `receiveShadow`. No shadow camera to set up. A spot light's own
lamp - anything whose bounds hold the light - doesn't block it, so a lamp's shade can cast shadows of
its own. A point light casts all round, and everything that casts blocks it, around it too: a candle in
a lantern or a carved pumpkin lights the room only through the openings. Give a bulb or flame mesh
drawn at the light `castShadow: false`. The directional shadow is fitted to whatever casts, every
frame; when things fly far off, give the light `shadowBounds: { min: [x, y, z], max: [x, y, z] }` -
the world area that gets shadows - so the map stays sharp there.

```js
scene.add(new PointLight({ position: [0, 0.1, 0], intensity: 0.5, range: 4, castShadow: true }))  // a candle in a jack-o'-lantern
```

**Product viewer passes** - three View options, each loading its code the first time it's on:

```js
const view = new View({ canvas, ambientOcclusion: true, groundShadow: true, fxaa: true })
scene.environment = 'studio'   // ambient occlusion dims light from all round: give the scene some
view.groundShadow = { opacity: 0.5, softness: 0.8 }   // change any time; false turns it off
```

- **`ambientOcclusion`** shades the creases - corners, gaps, under a lid, where things meet - from
  the picture's depth (screen-space, at half size). It dims only light from all round (ambient,
  hemisphere, environment), never the lights' direct light, and leaves unlit materials, points, lines
  and see-through things alone - so chart colours stay true. `strength` (default 1; an inside corner
  is about half in shade), `radius` in world units (default: a twentieth of the solids' size).
- **`groundShadow`** is the product viewer's soft floor shadow: the solids seen from below the
  ground, darkest where they touch it, blurred - no light or shadow map needed, and it shows with or
  without a floor mesh. Every opaque mesh casts it except floors that only receive shadows
  (`receiveShadow` on, `castShadow` off). `opacity` (0.6), `softness` (0-1, 0.5), `height` (how far up
  things still cast; default half the solids' size), `y` (the ground; default the solids' bottom),
  `size` (the shadow's square; default from the solids).
- **`fxaa`** smooths edges multisampling misses - cut-outs, shader detail - or all of them when
  `antialias: false` (cheaper on phones). Runs last, after bloom.
- Mistakes: a floor mesh that doesn't set `receiveShadow: true` casts a dark square of ground shadow
  - mark floors as receivers. Ambient occlusion with only directional lights shows nothing (there is
  no light from all round to dim). `view.explain()` names the effects on and warns about both.

Cameras: `new PerspectiveCamera({ fov, near, far, position, target })`,
`new OrthographicCamera({ height, near, far, position, target })` (width follows the aspect). Or
use a View camera preset: `'isometric'` and `'top'` are orthographic.

A plan view and back, for editors and floor plans:

```js
planButton.onclick = () => { view.camera = 'top'; view.controls.mode = 'map' }      // fitted, drags pan
threeDButton.onclick = () => { view.camera = 'perspective'; view.controls.mode = 'orbit' }
```

**Camera recipes** - the camera is moved by `frame()`, by its control, or by setting its `position`
and `target` yourself; the orbit always turns about wherever the target is.

- **Which way is up on screen**: from `'top'`, screen right is +x and screen up is -z (north on a
  map is -z). From `'front'`, right is +x and up is +y.
- **Fly to something**: `view.frame(node, { duration: 1 })` - the glide eases in and out, and a
  press or the wheel takes over.
- **Back to the start**: `view.frame(undefined, { direction: 'perspective', duration: 0.6 })`
  (or the preset the view started with).
- **Where framing would go**: `view.framing(target, { padding, direction })` returns
  `{ position, target, height? }` without moving the camera - for a camera that eases after
  something that keeps changing size (`camera.position.lerp(aim.position, 0.1)`, the same for target).
- **Follow something that moves** - move the camera and its target by as much as it moved, so the
  view keeps its angle and the user can still orbit round it:

  ```js
  let last = null
  view.start(() => {
    if (!followed) return
    const now = followed.updateWorld().worldPosition
    if (last) {
      const moved = now.clone().sub(last)
      view.camera.position.add(moved)
      view.camera.target.add(moved)
    }
    last = now
  })
  // to start: last = null; followed = planet; view.frame(planet) - and to stop, followed = null
  ```
- **Turn to an angle**: `view.controls.spherical = { yaw, pitch, distance }` (see Conventions).
- **Light far from a point light**: point and spot light falls off with the square of distance, so
  intensity scales with distance squared - a sun lighting planets 20 units away wants an intensity
  of about 400 and a `HemisphereLight` fill for their dark sides; things meant to glow regardless
  can be `unlit` or `emissive`.

## Interaction

```js
const view = new View({ canvas: '#c', orbit: true, highlight: '#ffffff',
  tooltip: (hit) => ({ title: hit.datum.name, rows: { Sales: hit.datum.sales } }) })
view.on('click', (hit) => { if (hit) select(hit.datum) })   // hit is null for empty space
view.on('hover', (hit) => show(hit?.datum))                 // fires when the thing under the pointer changes
```

- A **hit** is `{ node, instance, datum, point, distance, normal, face, uv }`. `datum` is the
  `data` row for the instance or point hit, or the node's own `data`.
- The **nearest surface** under the pointer is the hit - a link drawn over a site's top wins the
  hover there. To let one kind of thing through, give it `pickable: false`; to choose among
  everything under the pointer, `view.pickAll(event)` lists every hit, nearest first.
- **Selecting an area** - `view.pickArea({ x, y, width, height })` (width and height may be negative,
  as a drag up or left makes them) or `view.pickArea([[x, y], ...])` for a lasso: a hit for each point,
  instance and line segment whose place on screen is inside, and each mesh whose middle is. Places, not
  surfaces: what is hidden behind other things is found too, so a box over a scatter takes that whole
  region. Hidden, unpickable and zero-scale instances are left out. Turn `view.controls.enabled` off
  while the user drags out the area.

  ```js
  const chosen = view.pickArea({ x: 40, y: 30, width: 200, height: 120 }).map((h) => h.datum)
  ```
- **Rays of your own** - line of sight, what's below a dropped object, picking in tests: a
  `Raycaster` finds what any ray hits, on the CPU. Set `raycaster.ray.origin` and `.direction`, or aim
  it with `setFromCamera([x, y], camera)` (-1 to 1, y up); `intersect(nodeOrNodes)` returns hits,
  nearest first, as `pickAll` does. `threshold` (default 0.1, world units) is how near a ray must pass
  a point or line to hit it; `near` and `far` limit the distance.

  ```js
  const ray = new Raycaster()
  ray.ray.origin.set(0, 10, 0); ray.ray.direction.set(0, -1, 0)
  const ground = ray.intersect(view.scene)[0]   // what's straight below, or undefined
  ```
- **Tooltip** content: a string (new lines kept), an HTML element, or `{ title, rows }` with rows as
  an object `{ name: value }`. Return null for none. Styled by the `.phoria-tooltip` class.
- **highlight** tints the hovered node, instance or point. A drag never counts as a click.
- Per node: `tooltip`, `highlight`, `onHover`, `onClick` options on any node apply to it and its
  children. A node's `highlight` is the colour for its subtree; it tints the mesh, instance or point
  under the pointer. Add `highlightWhole: true` to tint the whole subtree as one thing (a piece of
  furniture, a machine) whichever part is hovered. Without the View's `highlight`, only nodes with
  their own highlight light up - leave it off to keep floors and walls plain, or keep it and give
  those `highlight: false` (`null` means "the View's").
- `onHover` and `onClick` are the app's own handler for a node; to add more without replacing it
  (an add-on, a second concern), `node.on('hover' | 'click', fn)` - it returns a function that stops
  listening. Both run. A drag has one handler, `onDrag`: one thing moves a node at a time.
- **Dragging**: `onDrag: (drag) => ...` on a node makes its subtree draggable. A press on it starts a
  drag (not an orbit) once the pointer has moved 4 px - until then it can still click - and the click
  after a drag is dropped. `drag` is `{ phase, hit, node, ray, plane, start, point, delta, event }`:
  `phase` is `'start'`, `'move'` or `'end'`; `point` is where the pointer's ray meets `plane`
  (null when it misses), and `delta` is `point - start`. `plane` (`{ normal, point }`) is
  horizontal through the hit unless the handler sets another at `'start'`. The cursor shows grab and
  grabbing.

```js
chair.onDrag = (drag) => {
  if (drag.phase === 'start') from = chair.position.clone()
  else if (drag.point) chair.position.copy(from).add(drag.delta)
}
```

- **Outline**: `outline: '#ffcc00'` or `{ color, width }` (pixels, up to 8; default 2) on a node draws
  a line round its silhouette, over everything - for what is selected, or as an inked edge for a
  drawn look. Set it any time; `null` removes it. Outlines are antialiased - soft edges and round
  corners - as the canvas is; `outlineAntialias: false` on the View (or `view.renderer.outlineAntialias =
  false`, any time) draws them in hard pixel steps instead.
- `view.controls.cancel()` lets go of the orbit gesture in progress, for apps that take over a press.
- **Keyboard and screen readers**: `keyboard: true` on the View makes the canvas a stop in the page's
  tab order. The arrow keys (and Home, End, PageUp, PageDown) step through what can be hovered or
  clicked, in scene order and each mesh's instances in order: each instance, point, surface grid
  point (a mesh with a row per vertex) or row of data under a node with its own `tooltip`, `onClick`,
  `onHover`, `onDrag` or `highlight` - and, when the View has a tooltip or handlers itself, each one
  with data. A mesh with no rows is a stop when it has a name or a handler of its own. A
  `highlightWhole` subtree is one stop. Lines with a row per segment (a network's links) are a stop
  per segment, after everything else. The one stepped to is shown as hovering would show it - tint (`#ffcc00` when no highlight
  is set), tooltip, hover handlers - and Enter or Space clicks it (the handler's event is null);
  Escape leaves it, and moving the pointer takes over. A screen reader hears each one: the tooltip's
  text, else its data, else its name, with "3 of 12" - or `keyboard: { label: (hit) => text }`. The
  canvas is labelled with `description`, or from the scene: each chart's `summary()` ("Sales: bar
  chart of 12 rows by month, sales"), else "3D view of 12 items".
- **Reduced motion**: `reducedMotion` follows the system's setting by default. When on, `frame()`
  with a `duration` jumps, `autoRotate` holds, and chart transitions and flowing links settle at
  once. Motion of your own (a `Timeline`, `onUpdate` spin) can check `view.reducedMotion`.

## Charts: `phoria2/charts`

```js
import { chart } from 'phoria2/charts'

const sales = view.scene.add(chart({
  mark: 'bar',
  data: rows,                         // [{ month: 'Jan', region: 'North', sales: 41 }, ...]
  x: 'month', z: 'region', y: 'sales',
  color: 'region',
  tooltip: ['region', 'month', { field: 'sales', format: { style: 'currency', currency: 'GBP' } }],
}))
view.frame(sales)
sales.update(newRows)                 // animates to the new data
```

A chart is a node with axes, ticks, grid walls, a legend and tooltips built in. Vega-Lite's shape
(`encoding: { x: { field, type } }`, `data: { values }`) is accepted as-is.

- **Marks**: `'bar'` (x and optional z bands, y value), `'point'` (scatter; x, y, z numbers or
  categories), `'line'`, `'area'` (a filled line; `stack: true` stacks series; with `y2` it fills between y and
  y2 - a band), `'surface'` (x, z grid
  with y heights), `'curve'` (a path through x, y and z in the order of its rows - an orbit, a GPS
  track; a path per `detail` value; `size` a number is its width in pixels), `'vector'` (arrows, from a
  function - below), `'network'`. There are no pie, donut or gauge marks - build those from
  `extrude` and `outline.arc`.
- **Channels**: `x`, `y`, `z`, `x2` (where a bar ends along x: bars span x to x2 on a number axis - a
  histogram's bins), `y2` (an area's other edge - a band such as a confidence interval - or where a bar
  starts, floating from y2 to y), `color`, `size`, `opacity`, `label` (text on each mark), `key` (row
  identity for animated updates; default `id`), `detail`. Each is a field name or
  `{ field, type, title, format, scale, axis, priority, legend }`, or a constant: `color: '#4e79a7'`
  (or `{ value: '#4e79a7' }`), `size: 0.2`.
  `scale`: `{ domain, range, scheme, zero, nice, type: 'linear' | 'log' }`; a colour field's `type` picks a ramp
  (quantitative) or a colour per value (anything else), and a ramp's domain can have more than two stops
  (`[0, 50, 100]` for a diverging scheme); schemes: `'category'`,
  `'viridis'`, `'blues'`, `'heat'`, `'cool'`, `'redblue'`, and `'hue'` - a colour wheel, the same colour at both
  ends, for angles that come back round (a phase, a direction, a time of day): give it the whole
  turn as its domain, `[-Math.PI, Math.PI]` or `[0, 360]`, and it wraps without a seam. `axis: false` or `{ title, format, ticks }`:
  `ticks` lists the values to mark (`[0, 25, 50, 75, 100]` - the axis reaches them) or says about how
  many (default 5).
- **Formats** (`format` on a channel, an axis or a tooltip field) are `Intl.NumberFormat` /
  `DateTimeFormat` options, or a function `(value) => string`:
  ``y: { field: 'sales', format: (v) => `£${v}k` }`` for values in thousands;
  `{ style: 'currency', currency: 'GBP', notation: 'compact' }` turns 42000 into £42K.
- **tooltip**: `true` (every encoded field), a field name, or a list of fields / `{ field, title, format }`.
  A field named on its own reads as the channel that encodes it - its `title` and `format` - so set
  those once, on the channel. The legend's title is the `color` channel's `title`.
- **Order**: bands follow the data's order, or `scale.domain` when given - `x` left to right, `z`
  front to back (the first `z` category is nearest the viewer). Put the tallest series at the back so
  it doesn't hide the rest: `z: { field: 'region', scale: { domain: ['West', 'South', 'North'] } }`.
- **Options**: `box: [x, y, z]` (the chart's size in world units, default about [10, 6, 6]),
  `stack: true` (bars with no `z` stack by `color`; areas stack), `width` (bar width share, 0-1),
  `legend: false | { position, container, ticks }` (`position`: `'top-right'`, `'top-left'`, `'bottom-right'`,
  `'bottom-left'` inside the canvas; `container`: an element or selector - the legend's HTML goes
  in it as a wrapping row, so give it no fixed height). Categories get swatches that click to hide
  and show; a number colour gets a key - a ramp, highest at the top, with values marked up its side,
  `ticks` as on an axis),
  `theme: 'dark' | 'light'`, `title`, `description` (what a screen reader hears for it; else `chart.summary()`
  makes one from the title and channels), `transition: false | { duration, ease }`,
  `overlap: 'dim' | 'hide' | 'show'` (labels), `highlight` (a colour, false, or for networks
  `'neighbours'` - the default, lighting the node's links and linked nodes - or `'node'`, the node alone),
  `equal` (the same units on x, y and z, so a shape keeps its proportions - the box takes the data's
  shape, its largest side the box's; default on for curves, parametric surfaces and vector fields),
  `frame: false` (no axes, grid walls or tick labels - a shape on its own) or `frame: 'origin'` (axes through
  zero with arrowheads and ticks, as on a blackboard - an axis not reaching zero crosses at its start),
  `contours` (surfaces: lines of equal height - `true` for about ten at the y axis's ticks, a count, or
  `{ count, values, place: 'surface' | 'floor' | 'both', color }`), and node options (`position`, ...).
- **Surfaces**: one row per grid point - `x` and `z` are the grid (numbers or categories), `y` the
  height; colour follows `y` unless `color` says otherwise:
  `chart({ mark: 'surface', data: rows, x: 'hour', z: 'day', y: 'load', color: { field: 'load', scale: { scheme: 'heat' } } })`.
- **Charts of a function** - `fn` and the ranges to sample it over, in place of data; sampled into rows
  (`hit.datum` is one), then drawn, coloured, tooltipped and tweened as any chart. JavaScript only - a
  function isn't JSON.

  ```js
  // a surface y = fn(x, z): ranges for x and z (x: [-3, 3], or { domain, title, axis }); y: [-1, 1] pins the value axis
  chart({ mark: 'surface', fn: (x, z) => Math.sin(x) * Math.cos(z), x: [-3, 3], z: [-3, 3], samples: 64 })
  // fn may give { y, ...fields }: the fields go on each row, to colour by - a complex function's size
  // as the height and its phase round the hue wheel (domain colouring)
  chart({ mark: 'surface', fn: (x, z) => ({ y: Math.hypot(x, z), phase: Math.atan2(z, x) }), x: [-2, 2], z: [-2, 2],
    color: { field: 'phase', scale: { scheme: 'hue', domain: [-Math.PI, Math.PI] } } })
  // a parametric surface [x, y, z] = fn(u, v) - a sphere, a torus; x, y and z come from fn - a range for one
  // (x: [-2, 2]) pins its axis, so shapes shown in turn share one box, each centred in it
  chart({ mark: 'surface', fn: (u, v) => [Math.cos(u) * Math.sin(v), Math.cos(v), Math.sin(u) * Math.sin(v)], u: [0, 2 * Math.PI], v: [0, Math.PI] })
  // a curve [x, y, z] = fn(t), coloured end to end unless color says otherwise
  chart({ mark: 'curve', fn: (t) => [Math.cos(t), t / 4, Math.sin(t)], t: [0, 12 * Math.PI], samples: 400 })
  // a vector field [vx, vy, vz] = fn(x, y, z): over x and z at y = 0, or a volume with a y range; coloured by magnitude
  chart({ mark: 'vector', fn: (x, y, z) => [-z, 0, x], x: [-2, 2], z: [-2, 2], samples: 9 })
  // y = fn(x) as a line or an area (200 samples by default); an area's fn may give [y, y2] to fill between two curves
  chart({ mark: 'area', fn: (x) => Math.sin(x), x: [0, Math.PI] })
  chart({ mark: 'area', fn: (x) => [Math.sqrt(x), x * x], x: [0, 1] })
  // a Riemann sum: samples rectangles across the x range (10 by default), each as high as fn at its
  // middle - rule: 'left' | 'mid' | 'right'; rows { x, x2, at, y }
  chart({ mark: 'bar', fn: (x) => x * x, x: [0, 2], samples: 8, rule: 'left' })
  // params: handed to fn as its last argument - change them and the chart tweens to the new shape
  const plot = chart({ mark: 'surface', fn: (x, z, { a }) => Math.sin(a * x), x: [-3, 3], z: [-1, 1], y: [-1, 1], params: { a: 1 } })
  plot.update({ params: { a: 2 } })      // or update({ fn }) - a new function on the same samples tweens too
  // time: true - fn gets the chart's clock as t, and only the mark is sampled again each frame (pin y)
  chart({ mark: 'surface', fn: (x, z, { t }) => Math.sin(Math.hypot(x, z) * 3 - t * 2), x: [-3, 3], z: [-3, 3], y: [-1, 1], time: true })
  ```

  `samples`: a number for every range or one each (`[64, 32]`); defaults 48 a side (surfaces), 64
  (parametric), 256 (curves), 9 (vector fields). Rows: surfaces `{ x, z, y }`, parametric
  `{ u, v, x, y, z }`, curves `{ t, x, y, z }`, fields `{ x, y, z, vx, vy, vz, magnitude }`, lines and areas
  `{ x, y }` (or `{ x, y, y2 }`), bars `{ x, x2, at, y }`. fn must give a
  finite value everywhere (clamp where it blows up) - an error names the point it didn't. Surfaces are
  shaded by normals worked out from fn, so they look smooth between samples (a sphere's poles too).
- **Curved coordinates** - `coords: 'polar' | 'cylindrical' | 'spherical'` (default `'cartesian'`): fn gives a
  radius (or a height) over angles - or rows of data give them, measured by angle - and the chart makes the
  points. theta turns from +x towards +z (away from the front, as a chart's z runs: anticlockwise seen
  from above) and defaults to all the way round; phi runs down from +y (0) to -y and defaults to top to
  bottom - the maths names (physics swaps theta and phi). Angles are radians, or degrees with
  `angles: 'degrees'` - ranges, what fn is handed, and the rows, all in degrees then. The long form,
  `angles: { units, zero, clockwise }`, also says where theta 0 points - `zero: 'right'` (the default),
  `'top'`, `'left'` or `'bottom'`; up the page for a polar curve, away from the front on the floor, as
  north on a map - and `clockwise: true` turns theta the other way: `{ units: 'degrees', zero: 'top',
  clockwise: true }` draws a microphone or antenna datasheet, or a compass bearing. The rings' angle
  labels follow. Equal units, and
  `frame: 'origin'` with faint rings round the origin like polar graph paper, unless `frame` says
  otherwise (`true`: walls, no rings). A negative radius is drawn through the origin, opposite.
  On a polar plot - and any plot of data - the rings are labelled with their values and the angles marked
  round the outermost every 30°, in place of the x and z axes (x and y for a polar curve; all three for
  data on a sphere). Give a channel - `x: { axis: { title } }` - to have its axis back.

  ```js
  // spherical: r = fn(theta, phi) - a sphere's bumps, spherical harmonics; coloured by r
  chart({ mark: 'surface', coords: 'spherical', fn: (theta, phi) => 1 + 0.2 * Math.cos(5 * theta) * Math.sin(phi) })
  // cylindrical: r = fn(theta, y), over a y range - a vase, a column
  chart({ mark: 'surface', coords: 'cylindrical', fn: (theta, y) => 1 + 0.3 * Math.sin(y * 2), y: [0, 4] })
  // polar surface: a height y = fn(r, theta) over a disc, over an r range
  chart({ mark: 'surface', coords: 'polar', fn: (r, theta) => Math.cos(r * 3) / (1 + r), r: [0, 4] })
  // polar curve: r = fn(theta), upright in the x-y plane, facing you - roses, cardioids, spirals
  chart({ mark: 'curve', coords: 'polar', fn: (theta) => Math.cos(3 * theta) })
  // a surface's fn may return { r, ...fields }: the fields go on each row, to colour by - here the
  // sign of an orbital's wave, drawn at its size
  chart({ mark: 'surface', coords: 'spherical', fn: (theta, phi) => { const y = Math.cos(phi); return { r: Math.abs(y), sign: y < 0 ? '-' : '+' } }, color: 'sign' })
  ```

  Rows: spherical `{ theta, phi, r, x, y, z }`, cylindrical `{ theta, y, r, x, z }`, polar surfaces
  `{ r, theta, y, x, z }`, polar curves `{ theta, r, x, y, z }`. `params`, `time`, `samples` and tweening
  work as above; a range for x, y or z pins that axis, as for parametric shapes.
- **Data by angle** - with `data`, theta, phi and r (and y, for a cylinder's height or a polar surface's)
  name fields of the rows instead of ranges: patterns measured round an antenna, a microphone, a lamp.
  `r: { field, scale: { domain: [lo, hi] } }` puts lo at the centre and hi on the outer ring - a dB floor -
  with what's beyond clamped there; the rings are labelled in r's own units. A surface's rows are a full
  grid of its two directions (an error names the first pair missing); angles a step short of all the
  way round (0-355°) are closed. A polar curve's rows are one path per series - `detail`, or a colour
  field of names - each in order of theta and closed if it goes round. Rows keep their own fields and
  gain x, y and z (a row's own x, y or z is refused - rename it); the tooltip shows the fields named.

  ```js
  // a 3D pattern: one row per direction - { azimuth, polar, gain } every 5°, gain in dBi
  chart({ mark: 'surface', coords: 'spherical', angles: 'degrees', data: rows, theta: 'azimuth', phi: 'polar',
    r: { field: 'gain', scale: { domain: [-20, 15] } }, color: { field: 'gain', scale: { scheme: 'heat' } } })
  // datasheet cuts: { pattern, angle, level } - one curve per pattern, on rings from -30 to 0 dB
  chart({ mark: 'curve', coords: 'polar', angles: 'degrees', data: rows, theta: 'angle',
    r: { field: 'level', scale: { domain: [-30, 0] } }, color: 'pattern' })
  ```

  Elevation (up from the horizon) is phi = 90 - elevation; an azimuth measured clockwise from north is
  `angles: { units: 'degrees', zero: 'top', clockwise: true }`.
  `update({ data })` with a grid of the same shape tweens.
- **Networks** - nodes as spheres and links as lines, laid out, labelled and interactive:

  ```js
  const services = [{ id: 'gateway', status: 'ok' }, { id: 'payments', status: 'down' }, ...]
  const calls = [{ source: 'gateway', target: 'payments' }, ...]   // link ends name node ids
  view.scene.add(chart({
    mark: 'network',
    data: { nodes: services, links: calls },
    color: { field: 'status', scale: { domain: ['ok', 'warning', 'down'], range: ['#2ecc71', '#f5a623', '#e74c3c'] } },
    label: 'id',                        // a name label on each node
    size: 'load',                       // optional: node size from a field
    link: { width: 2, color: '#8899aa' },   // or fields: width, color, opacity, flow (moving packets)
    layout: { tiers: 'tier', order: ['edge', 'service', 'data'] },   // or 'force' (default), or 'given' (x, y, z fields)
    highlight: 'neighbours',            // hover lights the node, its links and linked nodes; dims the rest
    tooltip: ['id', 'status'],
  }))
  view.on('click', (hit) => hit && show(hit.datum))   // the node's (or link's) row
  ```

  `source`/`target` name the link fields if they aren't called that; nodes are matched by `id`
  (or the `key` channel). Tiers run top to bottom, each tier a ring that widens further down - from
  the side (`camera: 'front'`, or a low view) they read as levels; `'force'` spreads nodes evenly
  instead. A hit on a node gives the node's row as `hit.datum`, on a link the link's row (it has
  `source` and `target`).
- **Chart object**: `update(rowsOrSpec)`, `filter(fn | null)`, `scales` (e.g. `chart.scales.y(50)`),
  `marks` (the nodes drawing it). Picking a mark gives the original row as `hit.datum`.
- **JSON Schema** for the spec ships with the package: `phoria2/charts/schema.json` - validate a
  spec before rendering it, or hand it to a model generating specs. It covers what JSON can hold: in
  code, `format` can also be a function and `legend.container` an element.

## Editing: `phoria2/edit`

For editors - planners, layout tools, scene builders: a handle to move and turn what is selected, and
undo. Built on `onDrag`, `outline` and `rayAt` above.

```js
import { TransformHandle, History } from 'phoria2/edit'

const history = new History({ onChange: (h) => { undoButton.disabled = !h.canUndo } })
const handle = new TransformHandle({
  view, history,
  snap: { move: 0.5, turn: Math.PI / 12 },               // a half-metre grid, 15 degree turns
  constrain: (placement, target) => fits(target, placement) ? placement : null,
  onChange: (target, phase) => showDistances(target, phase),
})
handle.target = chair                                    // null hides it
chair.outline = '#ffb000'
```
